summary.game: 70 rounds of rock-paper-scissors, Claude choosing every move by its own reasoning, one round per command, against an LSTM that retrains after each round on the player's full move history and plays the counter to its prediction.
how_it_went: Rounds 1-7: the AI plays randomly until it has data, so Claude played only rock to plant a habit.

Rounds 8-35 (20-4-4): Claude exploited the AI's slow early learning. Its percentages moved only a few points per round, so it kept expecting a move for ~2 rounds after Claude had switched away from it. Claude also read which move it had expected each round and hedged between its likely predictions.
Rounds 36-70 (13-10-12): much closer. The LSTM started recognising runs and learning Claude's own counter-habits (e.g. rock followed by scissors), and it became overconfident but sharper.
summary.verdict: Claude won clearly, because the match ended while the LSTM was still catching up. The trend in the second half suggests the edge would shrink with more rounds, which the 600-round match confirmed.

opponent: LSTM(16) -> dense(3, softmax), WINDOW=6, Adam, categoricalCrossentropy, 20 epochs per round on full history, TF.js 4.22 CPU (sim/play.js)
strategy_summary: Rounds 1-7 (AI still random): played only rock to plant a habit the model would learn and then be exploitable on.

Rounds 8-13: exploited training lag. Each round of training moves its probabilities only a few points, so after I switch moves it keeps expecting the old one for ~2 rounds; I switched just before its estimate flipped.
Round 14 on: after each round I read which move it had expected and built a map of its habits (e.g. after my rock it expected rock for a long stretch).
Hedging: when it was likely to pick one of two predictions, I played the move that beats one and ties the other, so I could not lose to either.
Safe-move detection: when one of my moves had near-zero predicted probability for several rounds, the AI never played that move's counter, so I could play it repeatedly without losing.

Weaknesses seen in the AI: slow adaptation early, strong overconfidence later (100% predictions that were wrong), and big confidence swings between rounds, which are signs of overfitting a small history.

Where it beat me: it recognized runs (three scissors) faster than I expected, and from ~round 30 it began modeling my own counter-habits (e.g. rock followed by scissors), so the second half was much closer than the first.
